title: Flood Fill: BFS/DFS from starting cell.
shortTitle: Flood Fill: BFS or DFS spreading from a starting cell
keyPoints: Flood Fill spreads a new value from a start cell to all connected cells sharing the original value
The critical early return guard is when newColor equals originalColor, preventing infinite loops
DFS marks the cell before recursing into neighbors; this prevents revisiting
BFS marks cells at enqueue time, not dequeue time, to prevent duplicate processing
Both approaches run in O(rows * cols) time and O(region size) space for the stack or queue
The same pattern applies to paint-bucket tools, region labeling, and risk-zone escalation

s1_definition.oneliner: Flood Fill spreads a new value outward from a start cell to all connected cells sharing the original value, using BFS or DFS, each cell touched once.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Flood Fill** repaints a connected region of same-color cells starting from a given cell.
- **DFS approach** recursively visits each same-color neighbor, repainting before recursing to prevent revisits.
- **BFS approach** uses a queue, enqueuing and repainting neighbors before dequeuing.
- **Critical guard** is the early return when newColor == originalColor, which prevents infinite recursion or infinite queueing.
- **Time** is O(rows * cols) in the worst case; **space** is O(region size) for the stack or queue.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the National Bank of India plotting a map of branches where each cell is a region with a risk rating. The risk team taps one region rated "medium" and says "reclassify this whole connected medium zone as high." The change spreads outward from the tapped region to every touching region that was also medium, like paint spreading across connected tiles, stopping where the rating is different.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flood Fill repaints a connected region of same-color cells starting from a given cell. The DFS version recursively visits each matching neighbor, repainting before recursing so that repainted cells stop matching and prevent revisits. The BFS version uses a queue and repaints at enqueue time to avoid duplicate processing.

The single most important guard is the early return when the new color equals the original color. Without it, every repainted cell still matches the original, so the recursion or queueing never stops. This one-line check is the difference between a correct solution and an infinite loop.

Both approaches run in O(region size) time because each cell in the connected region is visited exactly once. The DFS version is shorter but risks stack overflow on large regions; the BFS version uses a queue and avoids deep recursion. The same pattern powers paint-bucket tools, image region labeling, and minesweeper reveal logic.

At the National Bank of India, the risk team used Flood Fill to escalate an entire connected block of geographic zones sharing a risk code when a fraud cluster was confirmed. The early-return guard made the escalation safe to re-trigger, which mattered because the team sometimes clicked the same zone twice.

Remember one sentence: repaint before recursing so repainted cells stop matching, and always guard against newColor equaling originalColor to prevent infinite loops.
